# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Supervising Attorney]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 6, 2026
**Re:** Bougairt Pet Nutrition, Inc. / Drigask Holdings, LLC: Buyer and Note Maker exposure under the Stock Purchase Agreement and Exhibit B Seller Note

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed four documents:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement dated July 15, 2026 (the **SPA**);
- the March 18, 2026 Letter of Intent (the **LOI**);
- the agreed form of Seller Note at Exhibit B (the **Note**);
- the superseded Buyer draft of the Note dated June 2, 2026 (the **June Draft**).

The headline terms are:

| Term | Amount |
|---|---|
| Purchase Price (SPA §2.1) | $72,000,000 |
| Closing Cash Payment (SPA §2.2(a)) | $58,000,000 |
| Seller Note principal (SPA §2.2(b); Note §1) | $14,000,000 |
| Note interest (Note §2) | 6% simple, paid quarterly |
| Note maturity (Note §3) | 30 months after Closing |
| Seller General Cap (SPA §9.5(a)) | $7,200,000 |
| Purchase Price cap for Fundamental Representation and Product Recall Losses (SPA §9.5(c)) | $72,000,000 |

**The June Draft is not operative.** It is superseded. The operative instrument is the Exhibit B form, which is incorporated into the SPA by SPA §11.8 and must be delivered at Closing under SPA §3.3(b). The June Draft is still useful as drafting precedent: it already contains several of the fixes recommended below.

**Five issues need to go back to Drigask before Closing.** In order of priority:

1. **Note §4.2 caps recall and fundamental-rep recovery at the General Cap.** SPA §11.9 makes the Note control on recovery, so this eliminates the SPA §9.5(c) carve-outs.
2. **Seller rep survival is nine months (SPA §9.1).** The LOI said 18 months, and the products carry an 18-month shelf life. This also limits set-off under Note §4.1.
3. **The Fenwold change-of-control consent is not a closing condition (SPA §7.2(c)), and Seller is not required to seek it (SPA §6.4).**
4. **Buyer's Seller Guarantee indemnity (SPA §9.3(c)) is uncapped and has no time limit.** The definition of Seller Guarantees in SPA §1.1 is broad.
5. **The Note is freely transferable (Note §8) and carries monthly customer-level information rights (Note §5).** The LOI required Buyer consent to any transfer.

**Leverage.** The SPA is signed and the Note form is part of it, so every fix requires a written amendment signed by both parties (SPA §11.6). Seller has no contractual obligation to agree. Our practical leverage is limited to the following:

- the SPA tracks the LOI on most points, and these departures from it are easy to frame as drafting errors;
- Closing has not occurred and the December 31, 2026 outside date (SPA §8.1(b)) is approaching;
- Seller needs Buyer's cooperation to close cleanly, including on the Fenwold relationship, which matters to Seller's own valuation and to the Note's credit.

We should package the five points as a single amendment.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Note recovery cap overrides the recall and fundamental-rep carve-outs

**Location:** Note §4.2, read with SPA §§9.5(a), 9.5(c), 9.7 and 11.9.

**The problem.**

- **SPA §9.5(c)** removes Fundamental Representation claims and Product Recall Losses from the $540,000 deductible and the $7,200,000 General Cap. Those claims are capped at the $72,000,000 Purchase Price instead. This tracks LOI §6(d).
- **Note §4.2** says the aggregate Losses recoverable by Buyer Indemnitees under Article IX, "whether by set-off under this Note or otherwise, shall not exceed the General Cap, *including Losses described in Section 9.5(c)* of the Purchase Agreement."
- **SPA §11.9** would normally resolve a conflict in the SPA's favor. Here it does not, because it contains an express exception: "the Seller Note shall control with respect to set-off and recovery of indemnifiable Losses."

Note §4.2 is squarely a provision on recovery of indemnifiable Losses. Once the Note is issued at Closing, its restatement therefore governs. We should not assume the precedence clause rescues the carve-out. On a plain reading it does the opposite.

**Why it matters to Bougairt.**

- **Recall is the single largest exposure in a pet food acquisition.** A contamination or vitamin D recall covering several lots can easily exceed $7.2 million once retrieval, destruction, customer credits and Fenwold chargebacks are counted.
- **Title and capitalization claims are covered too.** Fundamental-rep claims, including title to the Shares, are cut to 10% of the price.
- **The cap reaches every recovery route.** Note §4.2 applies "by set-off … or otherwise," so it limits direct claims against Seller as well as set-off.
- **This is a departure from the deal.** The bargain in LOI §6(d) was a Purchase Price cap for these claims. Note §4.2 reverses it.

**Recommended fix.**

1. Replace Note §4.2 with language like June Draft §4.3: "Set-off under this Section 4 is subject to the deductible and the limitations on liability in Section 9.5 of the Purchase Agreement, as applicable to the claim in question." Delete the reference to Section 9.5(c).
2. Narrow SPA §11.9 so that the Note controls only the *mechanics* of set-off (timing, withholding, application and notice). Add an express statement that SPA §9.5 governs all limitations on liability and the amount recoverable.
3. Add a sentence to SPA §9.5(c) stating that nothing in any Transaction Document limits the carve-outs.

---

### Issue 2: Nine-month survival is too short for latent product claims

**Location:** SPA §9.1, read with SPA §4.14(c), LOI §6(b) and Note §4.1.

**The problem.**

- **SPA §9.1** says all non-fundamental Seller representations, *expressly including* the §4.14 product safety and recall representations, survive "until nine (9) months following the Closing Date." Claims must be noticed within that period.
- **LOI §6(b)** called for 18 months, expressly including the product safety and recall reps.
- **SPA §4.14(c)** says the Company's dry products have a shelf life of up to 18 months from manufacture.
- **Note §4.1** allows set-off only for claims noticed before the §9.1 survival period expires.

**Why it matters to Bougairt.**

- **The claim window closes while pre-Closing product is still on shelves.** Pre-Closing inventory with Pinecrest, its distributors and its retail customers can remain in the market for up to 18 months. A latent problem in that inventory, such as aflatoxin, a formulation error or excess vitamin D (the risks §4.14(a) itself names), may only appear through consumer complaints or regulatory sampling after month nine.
- **The set-off right lapses with it.** The Note runs 30 months, so Bougairt will hold roughly $14 million of Seller's money for 21 months after its claims against that money have expired.

**Interaction with Product Recall Losses.** The stand-alone §9.2(c) indemnity for Product Recall Losses is a covenant-type indemnity, not a rep. On its face it is not subject to the nine-month limit. However:

- the notice language in §9.1 and Note §4.1 is keyed to "the applicable survival period," and Seller will argue that the recall indemnity has none, or that it falls with §4.14;
- non-recall product-safety losses (claims, regulatory fines, lost business) depend on the §4.14 reps alone.

**Recommended fix.**

1. Restore general survival to at least 18 months, consistent with the LOI.
2. Extend survival of the §4.14 reps and the §9.2(c) recall indemnity through the later of 30 months after Closing (Note maturity) and final resolution of any noticed claim.
3. Amend Note §4.1 to allow set-off for any claim noticed within the applicable survival period *as so extended*. Also state that withholding for noticed but unresolved claims may continue past the Maturity Date.

**Facts needed from the client:**

- Was the nine-month period a negotiated trade during SPA drafting? If so, we need to know what Bougairt received in return before reopening it.
- Lot and manufacture-date data from Disclosure Schedule §4.14(c), to estimate how much pre-Closing product will still be in the market at month nine.

---

### Issue 3: Fenwold change-of-control consent is not a closing condition

**Location:** SPA §7.2(c) and §6.4, read with SPA §4.9(b) and LOI §7(d).

**The problem.**

- **SPA §4.9(b)** discloses that the Fenwold Supply Agreement is the Company's largest customer contract by revenue. A change of control needs Fenwold's prior written consent, and the agreement "may terminate upon a change of control" without it.
- **SPA §7.2(c)** conditions Buyer's obligation to close only on two consents: the Plant Lease landlord and the Equipment Financing lender. Fenwold is not listed, even though §7.2(c) uses the same "may terminate upon a change of control" language for those two contracts.
- **SPA §6.4** obliges Seller to seek only the consents listed in §7.2(c). Seller therefore has no covenant to approach Fenwold at all.
- **LOI §7(d)** made the Fenwold consent an express closing condition.

**Why it matters to Bougairt.**

- **Bougairt must close even if Fenwold refuses or terminates.** The rep bring-down in §7.2(a) does not help: §4.9(b) accurately discloses the consent requirement, so a refusal does not make the rep untrue.
- **No MAC condition fills the gap.** LOI §7(g) called for an MAC condition, but the SPA has none. Only the §4.7 rep is brought down, and it is qualified by materiality and dated from December 31, 2025.
- **There is no indemnity backstop either.** The risk is fully disclosed, so there is no breach to claim on.
- **Bougairt would pay full price and carry a $14 million Note** for a business that may have lost its largest customer.

**Recommended fix.**

1. Add a new §7.2(c)(iii): receipt of Fenwold's written consent to the change of control under the Fenwold Supply Agreement, in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to Buyer and without adverse modification of pricing, volume or term. This tracks LOI §7(d).
2. Conform SPA §6.4 and §3.2(b) so that Seller must use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the consent and deliver it at Closing.
3. Bar Seller from agreeing to concessions to Fenwold without Buyer's consent. SPA §6.1(c) already prohibits amending Material Contracts.
4. Fallback if Seller resists: a specific indemnity or a price reduction or Note reduction tied to Fenwold termination or non-renewal within a set period after Closing.

**Facts needed from the client:**

- Has anyone approached Fenwold, and how has Fenwold responded?
- What share of Company revenue and margin does Fenwold represent?
- When does the Fenwold Supply Agreement come up for renewal?

---

### Issue 4: Uncapped Buyer indemnity for Seller Guarantees

**Location:** SPA §9.3(c), read with SPA §1.1 (definition of "Seller Guarantees"), §6.8 and §9.5(b).

**The problem.**

- **SPA §9.3(c)** requires Buyer to indemnify Seller Indemnitees for all "Losses arising under any Seller Guarantee."
- **SPA §1.1** defines Seller Guarantees to include not only the guaranties scheduled in Disclosure Schedule §6.8 but also "any other guaranty, keep-well, letter of credit, surety bond or other credit support provided by Seller or any of its Affiliates for any obligation of the Company, *whether arising before or after the Closing*."
- **SPA §6.8** requires Buyer only to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain releases, and only for the scheduled guaranties.
- **The Buyer cap in SPA §9.5(b)** applies only to §9.3(a), Buyer's rep breaches. No cap, deductible or survival limit applies to §9.3(c).

**Why it matters to Bougairt.**

- **Bougairt has open-ended exposure to credit support it has never seen.** The definition reaches unscheduled support and pre-Closing obligations, and some of that support may never be released.
- **Seller's own liabilities can come back to Bougairt.** If a Seller guaranty is called because of a pre-Closing Company liability, such as a pre-Closing supplier claim, an environmental liability or a recall-related obligation, Seller can claim against Bougairt under §9.3(c). That is true even where Seller would itself owe Bougairt for the same underlying matter under §9.2.
- **Seller's recovery is uncapped while Bougairt's own claims are capped.** Seller could also use a §9.3(c) claim as leverage against Bougairt's set-off position under the Note.

**Recommended fix.**

1. Limit the "Seller Guarantees" definition to the guaranties specifically listed in Disclosure Schedule §6.8.
2. Limit §9.3(c) to Losses arising from Company obligations incurred *after* Closing.
3. Exclude from §9.3(c) any Losses arising from matters for which Seller indemnifies Buyer under §9.2 (pre-Closing liabilities, recalls, taxes, rep breaches), or for which Seller would do so but for the cap or deductible. Alternatively, provide an express offset.
4. Apply a cap (for example, the §9.5(b) $7,200,000 cap) and a time limit, ending on the earlier of release and a fixed date.
5. Fallback: Seller to identify all credit support before Closing, and any unidentified support is excluded from the indemnity.

**Facts needed from the client:**

- The contents of Disclosure Schedule §6.8.
- Any other Drigask credit support for the Company the client knows of, such as supplier guaranties, landlord guaranties under the Plant Lease, or Equipment Financing support.
- Whether the senior lenders will allow replacement credit support to be provided if releases are not obtained.

---

### Issue 5: Note is freely transferable and carries sensitive information rights

**Location:** Note §8 and §5, read with LOI §3(f) and SPA §6.10.

**The problem.**

- **Note §8** lets the Holder "sell, assign, pledge or otherwise transfer this Note, in whole or in part, to any Person *without the consent of Maker*." The Holder need only give notice within five Business Days *after* the transfer.
- **LOI §3(f)** said the Note would "[n]ot [be] transferable by Seller without Buyer's prior written consent." The June Draft §8.1 implemented that requirement and made non-consensual transfers void. The operative Exhibit B dropped it.

> To be clear: the operative Note at Exhibit B **does not** require Maker's consent to transfer. Only the superseded June Draft did.

- **Note §5** requires Bougairt to deliver to the Holder, monthly:
  - consolidated financials of Bougairt and its subsidiaries;
  - **customer-level sales reports for the Company showing net sales, volumes and gross margin by customer and product line.**

  It also gives the Holder an open-ended right to further information on request. These rights expressly benefit "each subsequent holder." There is no confidentiality or use restriction in the Note. By contrast, June Draft §5 limited reporting to quarterly and annual statements and imposed confidentiality and use limits.
- **SPA §6.6** (confidentiality) and **SPA §6.10** (non-compete and non-solicit) bind only Seller and its Affiliates. They would not reach an unaffiliated transferee.

**Why it matters to Bougairt.**

- **A competitor could buy the Note and receive Bougairt's commercial data every month.** Drigask could sell all or part of the Note to a competing pet food manufacturer or private-label co-packer. That buyer would then receive customer-by-customer margin data, including Fenwold pricing, for up to 30 months.
- **A hostile holder would hold the default and acceleration remedies (Note §9).** It could use any covenant default, including a late information delivery under §9.1(b), as a pressure point. Holders interested only in collection, such as distressed-debt buyers, are also more likely to contest set-off.
- **Partial transfers create practical problems.** They multiply counterparties for notices, set-off allocation and payments.
- **Senior lenders will also care** who holds subordinated debt.

**Recommended fix.**

1. Restore June Draft §8.1: no transfer without Maker's prior written consent, and any non-consensual transfer is void.
2. If Seller insists on liquidity, offer consent "not to be unreasonably withheld." That should be subject to:
   - an absolute bar on transfers to competitors of Bougairt or the Company, or their Affiliates;
   - no partial transfers;
   - the transferee confirming in writing, before the transfer is effective, that it takes subject to set-off and withholding under §4, subordination under §7, and confidentiality.
3. Add confidentiality and use restrictions to Note §5 along the lines of June Draft §5.
4. Cut the reporting back to quarterly and annual consolidated statements. Delete the customer-level reports in §5(b) and the open-ended request right in §5(d), or at least make them personal to Drigask so they do not pass to transferees.
5. Confirm that the Seller pledge right does not let Drigask's lenders take free of set-off.

**Facts needed from the client:**

- Whether Bougairt's senior credit agreement restricts transfers of subordinated debt or limits what information may be shared with junior creditors. Any Note change should be checked against the subordination agreement contemplated by Note §7.3.

---

## III. Other points for the client (lower priority)

- **No MAC closing condition.** LOI §7(g) included one. See Issue 3. Consider adding a general MAC condition to the same amendment.
- **Order of precedence generally.** Beyond Issue 1, any future Note revision should be reviewed against SPA §11.9, because the Note's recovery terms override the SPA.
- **Use of the June Draft.** The June Draft can be offered as the conforming text for Note §§4, 5 and 8, which lets us present these points as restoring agreed terms rather than new asks.

## IV. Next steps

1. Confirm the open facts flagged under Issues 2 through 5 with the client.
2. Prepare a single SPA amendment covering:
   - SPA §§1.1, 6.4, 7.2(c), 9.1, 9.3(c), 9.5 and 11.9;
   - a revised Exhibit B with conformed Note §§4.1, 4.2, 5 and 8.
3. Lead with Issues 1, 3 and 5 as clear departures from the LOI and Buyer's drafts. Present Issues 2 and 4 as risk-allocation corrections supported by the shelf-life disclosure and the breadth of the definition.
4. Raise the amendment promptly, since the December 31, 2026 outside date gives both sides a reason to resolve these points now.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Deal Team, Bougairt / Pinecrest Acquisition
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 6, 2026
**Re:** Buyer exposure under the signed Stock Purchase Agreement and the Exhibit B Seller Note, with proposed fixes for the next turn

---

## I. Summary

We reviewed four documents:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement signed July 15, 2026 (the "SPA");
- the March 18, 2026 Letter of Intent (the "LOI");
- the agreed form of Seller Note attached to the SPA as Exhibit B (the "Note"); and
- the superseded Buyer draft of the Note dated June 2, 2026 (the "June Draft").

The Purchase Price is $72,000,000. Of that amount, $58,000,000 is paid in cash at Closing, subject to the working capital adjustment, and $14,000,000 is paid through the Note. The Note is subordinated and unsecured. It bears 6% simple interest and matures 30 months after Closing.

Seller's indemnity for general representations is capped at the **$7,200,000 General Cap** under SPA §9.5(a), with a $540,000 deductible. Fundamental Representations and Product Recall Losses are carved out under §9.5(c) and capped at the Purchase Price.

**The June Draft is not operative.** The SPA incorporates Exhibit B as the agreed form (SPA §§2.2(b), 11.8), and Exhibit B is what Bougairt will sign at Closing. We use the June Draft below only as a source of fallback language that Bougairt previously proposed.

The SPA is signed, but Closing has not occurred. Every fix below therefore needs a written amendment under SPA §11.6, or an agreed revision of the Exhibit B form, executed before Closing. Our leverage now rests mainly on the fact that several items depart from the agreed LOI terms. It also rests on Seller's interest in closing before the December 31, 2026 outside date in SPA §8.1(b).

**Key issues, in priority order:**

1. Survival of non-fundamental representations, including product safety, is only nine months. This is half the LOI term and half the product shelf life. Set-off against the Note is cut off at the same point.
2. The Fenwold change-of-control consent is not a closing condition.
3. Bougairt's indemnity for Seller Guarantees is uncapped and has no time limit.
4. The Note is freely transferable, and the transferee receives sensitive monthly customer-level data.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: The nine-month survival period cuts off product safety claims and Note set-off

**Location:**
- SPA §9.1, which provides for survival "until nine (9) months following the Closing Date" and expressly includes the §4.14 representations.
- SPA §4.14(c), which states an 18-month shelf life for dry products.
- Note §4.1, which limits set-off to claims noticed within the §9.1 survival period.
- Compare LOI §6(b), which provided 18 months.

**Why it matters:**
- **Departure from the LOI.** LOI §6(b) set survival for general representations at 18 months after Closing and named the product safety and recall representations specifically. The SPA halves that period.
- **The period ends before the risk does.** Under SPA §4.14(c), Pinecrest's dry products carry a shelf life of up to 18 months from manufacture. Pre-Closing inventory will therefore stay in distribution and in consumers' homes long after the claim window closes. This includes finished goods held by distributors and retailers, as listed in Disclosure Schedule 4.14(c).
- **Latent defects surface late.** The defects the §4.14(a) representations target, such as aflatoxin contamination or vitamin D outside specification, typically appear through pet illness reports, FDA sampling or customer complaints well after manufacture. A defect in a lot made shortly before Closing could easily come to light 10 to 18 months after Closing.
- **Set-off ends at the same time.** Note §4.1 allows set-off only for claims noticed before the §9.1 survival period expires. Bougairt would lose its practical recovery source, the $14,000,000 Note balance, after month nine, even though the Note remains outstanding until month 30. After that point Bougairt would still owe full payment to Seller for a business whose product problems Seller had warranted against.
- **Interaction with the recall indemnity.** SPA §9.2(c) provides a standalone indemnity for Product Recall Losses. Seller is likely to argue, however, that recall-related claims grounded in a §4.14 breach are subject to the nine-month cutoff. The interaction is not clean, and we should not leave it to argument.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend SPA §9.1 to restore the LOI's 18-month general survival period.
- Separately, provide that the §4.14 representations and the §9.2(c) Product Recall Losses indemnity survive until at least 60 days after the Note Maturity Date. That is roughly 32 months, which covers the full shelf life of the last pre-Closing lots plus a reasonable discovery tail.
- Conform Note §4.1 so that set-off is available for any claim noticed within the applicable survival period as extended.
- State expressly that §9.2(c) claims are not subject to the general survival cutoff.

**Facts needed from client:**
- Pinecrest's historical lag between manufacture and complaint or recall events.
- The expected Closing date and the age profile of inventory at Closing.
- Whether QA diligence (lot testing records, complaint logs, FDA correspondence) turned up anything that argues for a special indemnity.

---

### Issue 2: The Fenwold change-of-control consent is not a closing condition

**Location:**
- SPA §4.9(b), which discloses that the Fenwold Supply Agreement requires Fenwold's consent and "may terminate upon a change of control" without it.
- SPA §7.2(c), which lists only the Plant Lease and Equipment Financing consents.
- SPA §6.4, under which Seller is obliged to seek only the §7.2(c) consents.
- SPA §3.2(b), which requires delivery of only the §7.2(c) consents.
- Compare LOI §7(d).

**Why it matters:**
- **Largest customer.** SPA §4.9(b) identifies the Fenwold Supply Agreement as Pinecrest's largest customer contract by revenue. The consent condition in LOI §7(d) was a specific, separately listed business point. It did not fall under the catch-all for "other required third-party consents."
- **No walk right.** As signed, Bougairt must close even if Fenwold refuses consent or signals it will terminate. The §7.2(c) list is closed, and nothing else gives Bougairt a walk right:
  - The bring-down condition in §7.2(a) does not help, because the change-of-control termination right is itself disclosed in §4.9(b). A Fenwold refusal is therefore not an inaccuracy in that representation.
  - The SPA has no MAE closing condition, even though LOI §7(g) contemplated one.
- **No obligation on Seller.** Seller has no covenant to approach Fenwold at all, because §6.4 covers only the listed consents.
- **No indemnity backstop.** If Fenwold terminates after Closing, the loss flows from a disclosed contract term. It is unlikely to support any indemnity claim against Seller.
- **Effect on the Note.** Bougairt would remain fully obligated on the $14,000,000 Note while absorbing the revenue loss.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend SPA §7.2(c) to add, as clause (iii), Fenwold's written consent to the change of control under the Fenwold Supply Agreement. The consent should be in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to Buyer and should confirm no adverse modification of pricing, volume or term. This tracks LOI §7(d).
- Conform §6.4 so that Seller must use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain the Fenwold consent, and conform §3.2(b) so that Seller must deliver it.
- Add a covenant that Seller will keep Buyer informed of, and let Buyer participate in, communications with Fenwold.
- Fallback, if Seller resists a hard condition: a specific indemnity, or a price reduction or Note reduction mechanism, triggered if Fenwold terminates or materially reduces purchases within an agreed period after Closing.

**Facts needed from client:**
- Whether anyone has approached Fenwold and what response, if any, has been received.
- Fenwold's share of revenue and gross margin.
- Whether Bougairt has its own relationship with Fenwold.
- Whether the client would close without Fenwold. The answer tells us how hard to push the condition versus the economic fallback.

---

### Issue 3: Bougairt's indemnity for Seller Guarantees is uncapped and open-ended

**Location:**
- SPA §9.3(c), under which Buyer indemnifies for "Losses arising under any Seller Guarantee."
- SPA §1.1, which defines "Seller Guarantees" as the guaranties in Disclosure Schedule 6.8 plus any other guaranty, keep-well, letter of credit, surety bond or credit support "whether arising before or after the Closing."
- SPA §9.5(b), whose Buyer cap applies only to §9.3(a).
- SPA §6.8, which imposes only an efforts obligation to obtain releases.

**Why it matters:**
- **Uncapped.** The $7,200,000 Buyer cap in §9.5(b) covers only breaches of Buyer's representations under §9.3(a). Nothing caps Bougairt's §9.3(c) liability.
- **No time limit.** §9.1 sets survival only for representations, and §9.3(c) is not tied to any survival period. The indemnity effectively runs indefinitely.
- **Reaches unknown and pre-Closing exposure.** Clause (b) of the definition reaches any credit support by Seller or its Affiliates for any Company obligation, whether or not scheduled, and whether arising before or after Closing. Bougairt would be underwriting guaranties it has never seen. That could include support for pre-Closing liabilities that are Seller's responsibility under the SPA, such as pre-Closing Taxes under §9.2(d) or Product Recall Losses under §9.2(c).
- **Circularity.** If a Seller guaranty covers a Company obligation that arose from a pre-Closing product problem, Seller could call on Bougairt under §9.3(c) for the same Losses Seller owes Bougairt under §9.2. Seller's obligation is capped and time-limited; Bougairt's is not.
- **Efforts covenant only.** Under §6.8 Bougairt only has to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain releases and need not pay fees or post replacement support. Unreleased guaranties could therefore remain outstanding indefinitely, with Bougairt as the backstop.

**Recommended fix:**
- Narrow the §1.1 definition of "Seller Guarantees" to the guaranties actually listed on Disclosure Schedule 6.8, and delete clause (b).
- Limit §9.3(c) to Losses arising from obligations of the Company first arising after the Closing, under Contracts disclosed to Buyer.
- Add an express exclusion for any Losses for which Seller is obligated to indemnify Buyer Indemnitees under §9.2, or that relate to pre-Closing periods.
- Cap the §9.3(c) exposure, for example at the amount of the scheduled guaranteed obligations or alongside the §9.5(b) cap.
- Have it terminate on the earlier of release of the guaranty or expiry of the underlying obligation.

**Facts needed from client:**
- The current contents of Disclosure Schedule 6.8.
- Whether diligence identified any unscheduled credit support by Drigask, such as letters of credit for leases, supplier guaranties or surety bonds for feed licenses.
- Whether Bougairt's senior lenders will let it provide replacement credit support, which would make full releases achievable.

---

### Issue 4: The Note is freely transferable, and the transferee receives Bougairt's customer-level data

**Location:**
- Note §8, under which the Holder may transfer "to any Person without the consent of Maker."
- Note §5, which provides monthly financials, monthly customer-level sales reports and open-ended information requests "for the benefit of Holder and each subsequent holder."
- Compare LOI §3(f) and June Draft §§5, 8.

**Why it matters:**
- **Departure from the LOI.** LOI §3(f) provided that the Note would not be transferable by Seller without Buyer's prior written consent. The operative Exhibit B reverses this. Bougairt's consent was required in its own June Draft, but that draft is superseded and gives Bougairt no protection.
- **Sensitive information goes with the Note.** Note §5 requires Bougairt to deliver every month:
  - consolidated financial statements; and
  - Pinecrest's net sales, volumes and gross margin broken out by customer and product line.

  It also allows Holder to request "such other information" as it reasonably requests. These rights expressly benefit each subsequent holder.
- **No confidentiality obligation.** The Note contains no use restriction or confidentiality covenant. The June Draft's confidentiality language in its §5 was dropped.
- **The non-compete does not reach a transferee.** SPA §6.6 confidentiality and the §6.10 non-compete bind only Seller and its Affiliates. An unaffiliated competing pet food manufacturer, or a distressed-debt buyer that shares information, could acquire the Note and receive Bougairt's pricing and margin data by customer month after month.
- **Remedies go with the Note.** A transferee would also hold the Note's default and acceleration rights under §9 and could enforce aggressively against Bougairt. Transferees take subject to set-off and subordination under §8, but a partial transfer would split the Note among several holders. That would complicate set-off notices and withholding under §4.
- **Senior lender consent.** Bougairt's senior lenders may also object to an unknown subordinated creditor.

**Recommended fix:**
- Replace Note §8 with the LOI position: no sale, assignment, pledge or transfer by Holder, in whole or in part, without Maker's prior written consent, and any non-compliant transfer void. June Draft §8.1 is a ready starting point.
- If Seller insists on some flexibility for estate-planning or Affiliate transfers, permit transfers to wholly owned Affiliates of Seller that remain bound by SPA §§6.6 and 6.10. In every case, prohibit transfers to any Person engaged in the manufacture or sale of pet food, and to any Affiliate of such a Person.
- Require each transferee to confirm in writing, before the transfer is effective, that it is bound by the set-off right, the subordination provisions and a confidentiality and use restriction (see June Draft §8.2).
- Separately, scale back Note §5:
  - deliver quarterly consolidated financials, as in June Draft §5(a), rather than monthly;
  - delete the customer-level sales reports in §5(b) and the open-ended request right in §5(d); and
  - add the June Draft's confidentiality and use restriction.

**Facts needed from client:**
- Whether Bougairt has any commercial need to accept the §5 reporting package, for example because Seller asked for it to monitor credit.
- Whether the senior lenders' intercreditor terms will restrict Note transfers in any event.

## III. Points of Leverage and Approach

- Issues 1, 2 and 4 are departures from the LOI. The LOI is non-binding on these terms under LOI §12, but the agreed business deal is the strongest basis for asking Seller to amend a signed SPA. We should present them as conforming changes.
- Issue 3 is not addressed in the LOI. We should frame it as a drafting overreach in the definition, and point to the circularity with Seller's own §9.2 obligations.
- All changes should be documented in a single SPA amendment, with a revised Exhibit B attached, executed well before the December 31, 2026 outside date.
